passage: Jahnavi, sit. You think your Akash mama was always this calm? When I was twenty, my hostel roommate copied my project and submitted it before me. The professor believed him, not me. For a week I lay awake replaying that meeting, planning how to let the air out of his bike tyres, how to post his old messages to the whole class. One night I wrote everything in a notebook instead, every ugly plan, and locked it in my trunk. Next morning I went to my friend Deepak's room and talked until the tea went cold. He didn't tell me to calm down; he just listened. Then I started running at five every morning and poured the rest into my exams. Beta, the anger was real. I let it out on paper and on the track, not on his tyres. That is why I have nothing from that year to apologise for.

qa.q: What did Akash write in the notebook?
qa.a: He wrote every ugly plan, and then locked the notebook in his trunk.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling during the week he lay awake?
qa.a: He felt hurt and furious that the professor believed his roommate, and the anger kept replaying the meeting and building revenge plans.

qa.q: What turning point did Akash use at this stage, and why did it work?
qa.a: He let the anger out safely by writing the plans privately, talking to Deepak and then running and studying, so the feeling was spent without adding new harm.

qa.q: How might Deepak have experienced the morning Akash came to talk?
qa.a: Deepak probably saw a friend boiling with anger and chose to listen rather than lecture, which let Akash feel heard instead of judged.

grounding: Shows replayed hurt and revenge fantasies being written down privately, shared with a trusted friend and channelled into running and study so no new harm follows.

passage: The power went out again at nine, and Lalit sat in the dark of the one-room flat he shared with his two younger brothers, phone at eight percent. Santosh's forward still sat on the screen: Lalit's private worry about failing maths, sent to the whole class group as a joke. For two days Lalit had replayed it, drafting replies that would humiliate Santosh back, imagining telling Santosh's parents the secret Santosh had once trusted him with. With the battery dying, he tore a page from his rough book and wrote it all out by candlelight, then folded it into his pocket. He texted Meher, his oldest school friend: 'Can I call tomorrow? I'm so angry it scares me.' She rang early and let him talk for twenty minutes. Afterwards he walked to the ground and ran laps until his legs shook, then opened the maths book Santosh had mocked.

qa.q: Where did Lalit write out his anger?
qa.a: On a page torn from his rough book, by candlelight.

qa.q: What does Lalit's message to Meher suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was frightened by how strong his anger had become and wanted help before it turned into something he would regret.

qa.q: Which choices at this stage kept Lalit's anger from causing new harm?
qa.a: Writing it all out on paper, calling Meher, and then running and studying let the anger move through him instead of into a cruel reply or a betrayed secret.

qa.q: What might Meher be experiencing when Lalit calls her?
qa.a: Meher may feel trusted and a little worried for him, and by simply listening she gives him a safe place to let the anger out.

grounding: Illustrates the replay-and-revenge stage handled by a private written note, a talk with a trusted friend and running and study, despite a power cut and a crowded room.

subtype: Stage 5: Deciding to release the grudge [Response]
passage: Rain ticked on the tram window as Santiago rode home from the bakery in Porto, flour still under his nails. Two years ago Kofi had walked out of their food-truck plan a week before opening, taking the van deposit with him and never explaining. Santiago had rehearsed the phone call a hundred times. Tonight, at the kitchen table, he wrote a letter instead. You left me with debts and a lot of silence. I was angry for a long time. I'm putting this down now. He read it twice, then placed it in the drawer, not in an envelope. Kofi had never said sorry, and maybe never would. Santiago noticed he was tired of waiting for that. He made tea, texted his sister that he would come to her barbecue on Sunday, and for the first time in months fell asleep without rehearsing anything.

qa.q: Where did Santiago put the letter after reading it?
qa.a: He placed it in the drawer, not in an envelope.

qa.q: What was Santiago feeling when he noticed he was tired of waiting?
qa.a: He felt worn out by carrying the resentment and ready to set it down for his own peace, even without an apology from Kofi.

qa.q: Why was writing the letter without sending it a useful step for Santiago?
qa.a: It let him say everything he felt and mark an ending on his own terms, without needing Kofi to answer or apologise first.

qa.q: What is Santiago's sister likely to notice about him after this night?
qa.a: She may find him lighter and more present at her barbecue, because he is no longer stuck rehearsing an old phone call.

grounding: Shows a person choosing to put down a grudge for their own peace through a letter that is never sent, with no apology from the other person.

subtype: Stage 5: Deciding to release the grudge [Response]
passage: 'She still hasn't said a word,' Kiran said, turning the paper cup in her hands. The staff wellbeing room at the district hospital smelled of disinfectant and cardamom tea. Eight months ago Salma, the charge nurse, had blamed Kiran in front of the whole ward for a missed chart entry, and the entry had been Salma's own. The counsellor asked what holding on to it was giving her. Kiran thought. 'Every shift I check whether she's on the rota. I rehearse what I'd say. I'm the one losing sleep.' She was quiet for a while. 'I don't need her to admit it. I just want my shifts back.' She didn't text Salma or ask for a meeting. She walked back to Ward 4, took the handover sheet, and when she saw Salma's name on the rota she only nodded and started her rounds.

qa.q: Who had actually made the missed chart entry?
qa.a: The entry had been Salma's own.

qa.q: What does Kiran's habit of checking the rota suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: It suggests the resentment had been ruling her working days; she was tense, rehearsing lines and losing sleep over it.

qa.q: What helped Kiran decide to let the grudge go?
qa.a: The counsellor's question about what holding on gave her showed Kiran that she was the one paying, so she chose release without waiting for Salma to admit anything.

qa.q: How might Salma experience Kiran's calm nod on the ward?
qa.a: Salma may be surprised or unsure what changed, since Kiran is no longer tense around her; the air between them is likely less charged.

grounding: Illustrates deciding to release a grudge by talking it through, for one's own peace and without an apology from the person who caused the hurt.

passage: Hi, I'm Uday, and this is the part of the podcast where I overshare. You asked where Harsha and I stand. Last year, when we shared a flat, he read my messages while I slept and told my manager I was job hunting. I lost the promotion. It took me months to stop being furious. Then in March he came to my door, no excuses, and said he'd been jealous and it was wrong. He had already told my manager the truth; I checked. So yes, I've forgiven him, and I mean it. But forgiving him isn't the same as handing him my phone again. We meet for chai on Sundays, in public, for an hour. I don't share work news yet. If he keeps showing up the same way, maybe that grows. If he slips, I step back, and I won't feel guilty about it.

qa.q: How long do Uday and Harsha meet for on Sundays?
qa.a: An hour, in public, for chai.

qa.q: Why does Uday still keep work news from Harsha after forgiving him?
qa.a: Uday's trust was broken when Harsha went to the manager, and forgiving did not bring it back, so Uday wants to see steady behaviour first.

qa.q: What choice at this stage lets Uday rebuild without risking new harm?
qa.a: Rebuilding slowly with clear limits: short public meetings, no work news for now, and a plan to step back without guilt if Harsha slips.

qa.q: What might Harsha be experiencing in these Sunday meetings?
qa.a: Harsha may feel grateful for the second chance but also aware that the limits are there because his remorse has to be shown over time.

grounding: Shows forgiveness without a return to full trust: after real remorse, the person chooses to rebuild slowly and keeps the right to step back.

passage: I'm Nitin, and I sit next to Hafsa at the design studio, so I see more than I'm meant to. Her ex-boyfriend Imran turned up at reception again on Thursday with flowers and the same line: he'd forgiven her for making him angry. Last year he shouted at her in the parking lot until security walked over. I watched Hafsa go down and speak to him for maybe a minute, calm, not smiling. She came back up without the flowers. 'I've forgiven him,' she told me, pouring water. 'I'm not angry every day anymore. But he still thinks it was my fault. So no coffee, no calls.' Then she asked reception to ring her before letting him up next time. I don't know what she felt inside. Her hands were steady, though, and she finished the logo draft before lunch.

qa.q: What did Hafsa ask reception to do?
qa.a: To ring her before letting him up next time.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's remark that Imran still thinks it was her fault show about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she noticed he has no real remorse, so she has decided that forgiving him does not mean letting him close again.

qa.q: Why is keeping distance a wise choice for Hafsa at this stage?
qa.a: Imran shouted at her before and still blames her, so staying away protects her safety while she lets go of the daily anger.

qa.q: How does Nitin see Hafsa's handling of Thursday's visit?
qa.a: Nitin sees calm, steady behaviour but admits not knowing what Hafsa felt inside; the steady hands and finished draft are the only clues.

grounding: Illustrates that forgiveness can sit with keeping distance when the other person shows no remorse and has caused harm.

passage: After the shift ended on the training floor of the Pune call centre, Avni stayed behind, laptop open to an email she had rewritten four times. Last Tuesday she had told the whole team that the missed client deadline was Kashish's fault. It was hers; she had forgotten to forward the file. Kashish had been quiet all week. Avni sent the email to the team: 'The delay was my mistake, not Kashish's. I'm sorry.' Then she found Kashish at the vending corner, said it again face to face, and asked how to make it right. Kashish shrugged, then said, 'Maybe tell the manager too.' Avni did, that evening. On the bus home the old voice started: you're careless, you ruin everything. She wrote down one change instead, a shared tracker for files, and let herself stop there.

qa.q: What change did Avni write down on the bus?
qa.a: A shared tracker for files.

qa.q: What does the voice on the bus reveal about how Avni felt after apologising?
qa.a: It shows she still felt shame and was tempted to keep punishing herself, calling herself careless even after making amends.

qa.q: How did Avni turn guilt into repair instead of endless shame?
qa.a: She owned the mistake to the team, apologised to Kashish in person, told the manager, and then chose one concrete change instead of replaying the blame.

qa.q: What might Kashish have been going through during the week before the email?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt wrongly blamed and embarrassed in front of the team, which could explain being quiet all week.

grounding: Shows a person who caused harm owning it, making amends and choosing one change instead of endless self-punishment.

passage:
Dear Vijay,
It's been a year since Papa's retirement dinner, when I told everyone you'd never finish anything. I said it for a laugh. You left before dessert.
I've thought about that night more than you'd guess. For months I just felt awful and did nothing, as if feeling bad was enough. It wasn't.
So here's what I have done. I told Mummy and Papa that what I said was unfair and untrue. I went to your pottery show last month and stood at the back; the photos I took are in this envelope.
I'm sorry. You don't have to reply.
I'm also trying to stop calling myself the worst sister alive. That doesn't help you either. What helps is me being kinder at the next dinner, and the one after.
Love,
Preeti didi

qa.q: When did Preeti say the hurtful words to Vijay?
qa.a: At Papa's retirement dinner, a year ago.

qa.q: What does Preeti mean when she writes that feeling bad was not enough?
qa.a: She realises that months of guilt without action did nothing for Vijay, and she wants her regret to turn into repair.

qa.q: Which of Preeti's steps turn guilt into amends?
qa.a: Correcting her words with Mummy and Papa, going to Vijay's pottery show and apologising without demanding a reply are all real repair.

qa.q: What might it be like for Vijay to receive this letter?
qa.a: Vijay may feel surprised and partly relieved that Preeti set the story straight with Mummy and Papa, though Vijay may still need time, and the letter leaves Vijay free not to reply.

grounding: Illustrates self-forgiveness after causing harm: owning it, making amends and choosing growth over endless shame.

passage: Plastic chairs lined the hall above the sweet shop in Bhadrak, and Arohi arrived in her work kurta, straight from the block office where she typed land records. Kamal was already there, telling everyone about his master's in Germany and the flat he rented in Munich. Pooja passed around wedding photos. Rakesh had opened a solar-pump business with twelve employees. Someone asked Arohi, 'Still at the block office?' She said yes and laughed, and the laugh came out thin. She kept her phone face-down on her lap. When the samosas came round she took one and forgot to eat it. On the auto home, past the same paddy fields she had seen every day since school, she counted: no degree abroad, no husband, no business. At twenty-five, her life suddenly looked like a small room she had wandered into by mistake.

qa.q: Where did Arohi work?
qa.a: At the block office, where she typed land records.

qa.q: How can you tell that Arohi felt shaken at the reunion?
qa.a: Her laugh came out thin, she kept her phone face-down and forgot to eat her samosa, then counted everything she lacked on the way home.

qa.q: What could help Arohi at this early stage, before the comparison hardens?
qa.a: Talking it over with someone she trusts, and remembering that a reunion shows only highlights, could stop one evening from deciding how she sees her whole path.

qa.q: How might Kamal have experienced the same evening?
qa.a: Kamal probably enjoyed sharing his news and may not have noticed how it landed on Arohi; to him it was catching up, not comparing.

grounding: Shows the sudden comparison shock of a 25-year-old at a reunion when classmates' degrees, marriages and businesses make her own path feel small.

passage: Sunday night, Camila lay on the sofa of her shared flat in Valencia, scrolling a photo app with her thumb. Nour, her old roommate from university, had posted a ring and a sunset. Two swipes later, a classmate announced a startup that had just raised money. Another had a new apartment with a balcony in Amsterdam. Camila was twenty-five, teaching evenings at a language school and still splitting rent three ways. She typed 'congrats!!! 😍' under Nour's post, deleted it, typed it again. Her chest felt tight. She looked around the room: the drying rack of laundry, the chipped mug, the plant she kept forgetting to water. A few hours earlier those things had felt fine, even cosy. Now they looked like proof she had fallen behind. She turned the phone over and stared at the ceiling until the fridge stopped humming.

qa.q: Where did Camila work?
qa.a: At a language school, teaching evenings.

qa.q: What does Camila deleting and retyping her comment suggest?
qa.a: It suggests mixed feelings: she wanted to be glad for Nour but was stung by the comparison 😔

qa.q: What small step could help Camila at this point?
qa.a: Putting the phone away for the night and talking to a friend about the sting, rather than lying alone with it, could keep the shock from growing.

qa.q: How might Nour see Camila's congratulations comment?
qa.a: Nour would likely read it as warm and happy, with no idea of the tight chest behind it.

grounding: Illustrates comparison shock on social media, where friends' engagements, startups and new homes suddenly make a 25-year-old's own life feel late.

subtype: Stage 2: Counting the roads not taken [Actor]
passage: Jeevan cut the motor at the canal and sat on the bund while the water spread slowly across the paddy. Twenty-five, he thought, and still in these fields. The bus to Mysuru passed on the road above, the same bus his classmate Rashmi had taken six years ago to join her nursing course. She had begged him to apply with her. He hadn't, because Appa's knee was bad and Amma cried at the thought of him leaving. Then there was the electronics diploma he dropped after one term, and the girl from the next village he never spoke to properly because his uncles were always watching. He counted them on muddy fingers: the course, Rashmi's bus, the girl, the lost year. Only the last felt like his own laziness. The rest had been decided by fear of disappointing someone, and that made them sting more, not less.

qa.q: Why didn't Jeevan apply with Rashmi?
qa.a: Because Appa's knee was bad and Amma cried at the thought of him leaving.

qa.q: Why do the chances decided by fear sting Jeevan more than the lost year?
qa.a: He feels those choices were never truly his; they were made to avoid disappointing others, so they carry regret and a sense of lost freedom.

qa.q: What could help Jeevan at this stage of counting losses?
qa.a: Sorting which chances are truly gone from those he could still revisit, and talking honestly with Amma and Appa about what he wants, could give the regret somewhere to go.

qa.q: How might Amma see Jeevan staying on the farm?
qa.a: Amma may see it as her son staying close and safe, without knowing how much he gave up to spare her tears.

grounding: Illustrates counting the roads not taken, where regret is sharpest for choices shaped by family worry and fear rather than desire.

passage: At her cousin's christening lunch in Cebu, Rosa counted the questions. Tita Lorna asked when she'd bring someone home. Tito Ben asked whether the bank teller job had a pension. Her grandmother patted her hand and said, 'Before thirty, anak, or the good ones are gone.' Rosa smiled through all of it, then locked herself in the bathroom and did the maths: meet someone this year, date for two, marry at twenty-eight... It already felt too late. Her savings were small. Cousins her age had babies on their hips. She texted Tariq, her friend from work: 'Everyone here has a timeline for me and I'm failing all of them.' He wrote back, 'Whose timeline, though?' Rosa stared at that, washed her face, and went back out for cake, still counting.

qa.q: What did Rosa's grandmother tell her?
qa.a: 'Before thirty, anak, or the good ones are gone.'

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when she did the maths in the bathroom?
qa.a: Panic that time was running out; every step of the imagined timeline made her feel she was already too late 😰

qa.q: What opening does Tariq's reply give Rosa at this stage?
qa.a: His question 'Whose timeline, though?' invites her to see the deadline as her family's clock rather than a rule, which could loosen the sense of failure.

qa.q: How might Rosa's grandmother see her own advice?
qa.a: She likely means it as loving protection drawn from her own era's expectations, without seeing how heavily it lands on Rosa.

grounding: Shows the fear of being behind as family questions set a deadline for marriage and money, making ordinary variation feel like failure.

passage: The box of kaju katli went from desk to desk at the bank branch, and Damini followed it, glowing, holding out her phone with the engagement photo. Tanvir took a piece and said the right things. Then Mr Rao, the branch manager, leaned over: 'Your turn next, Tanvir? You're what, twenty-five? My son was settled by then.' Everyone laughed. Tanvir laughed too. At lunch he checked his account balance twice, then opened the message from Ammi with three biodata photos. His whole mohalla seemed to move in one direction on a fixed calendar, and he was standing still. By evening his chest was tight. He stayed late reconciling ledgers, not because they needed it, but because at home Ammi would ask again, and he had no answer that sounded like enough.

qa.q: What did Mr Rao ask Tanvir?
qa.a: 'Your turn next, Tanvir? You're what, twenty-five?'

qa.q: Why did Tanvir stay late reconciling ledgers?
qa.a: He was avoiding Ammi's questions because he feared his life would not sound like enough by his community's calendar.

qa.q: What turning point could help Tanvir at this stage?
qa.a: He could name the pressure to someone he trusts and ask whether that fixed calendar is really his; a calm talk with Ammi about his own plans might ease the dread.

qa.q: What might Damini be experiencing as her news goes round the branch?
qa.a: Damini is excited and sharing her joy, probably unaware that the celebration adds weight to Tanvir's day.

grounding: Illustrates the fear of being behind at 25 when a workplace joke and a tight-knit community's marriage timeline make a normal pace feel like failure.

passage:
'I'm quitting tomorrow,' Irawati said, dropping her bag by the door.
Asif, her flatmate, looked up from the stove. 'Tomorrow? What happened?'
'Nothing happened. That's the problem. Same desk, same spreadsheets, same bus. I could move to Goa. Rent a room, teach surfing, whatever.'
'You don't surf.'
'I'd learn!' She pulled out her phone. 'Look, I've already found three rooms.'
'Iru, last month it was Canada. Before that, breaking up with Nikhil.'
She sat down hard. 'I know. I just feel like I'm dissolving.'
'Okay.' He turned the gas down. 'What would Goa give you?'
'Sea. Time. Not being bored out of my skull.'
'And if you quit tomorrow, what pays the rent there?'
She didn't answer. She scrolled the rooms again, slower.
'I'm not saying stay,' Asif said. 'I'm saying find out what you're hungry for first.'

qa.q: Where did Irawati say she could move?
qa.a: To Goa, to rent a room and teach surfing.

qa.q: What does 'I just feel like I'm dissolving' reveal about Irawati?
qa.a: It shows the urge to quit comes from feeling empty and bored, as if she is losing herself, rather than from a clear plan.

qa.q: What question helps turn Irawati's restlessness into useful information?
qa.a: Asif's question, 'What would Goa give you?', helps her name the needs behind the urge (sea, time, not being bored) so she can look for ways to meet them without a sudden leap.

qa.q: What might Asif be feeling as he hears about Goa?
qa.a: Asif seems concerned but patient; having heard about Canada and the breakup before, he wants to help Irawati find what is missing rather than brush her off.

grounding: Shows sudden urges to quit, move or break up as a signal of unmet needs, and how an overnight leap might not meet them.

passage: My name's Baljeet, and last winter I nearly blew up my whole life in one weekend. It started on a Friday when my manager pushed my leave back again. By Saturday night I had a resignation email drafted, a one-way bus ticket to Shimla open in another tab, and a speech ready for Kiran about how we'd grown apart. None of it had existed on Thursday. I remember pacing the balcony at 2 a.m., feeling like a door would slam shut on me forever unless I ran first. On Sunday morning I told Kiran everything, even the speech. Kiran listened, then asked what I had actually been missing. The honest answer was mountains, rest, and a job that didn't own my weekends. Not the end of us. I didn't send the email. Looking back, the urge was real; the plan just aimed at the wrong target.

qa.q: What did Baljeet have open in another tab?
qa.a: A one-way bus ticket to Shimla.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling while pacing the balcony at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Trapped and panicked, as if a door would slam shut forever unless Baljeet ran first.

qa.q: What helped Baljeet avoid an impulsive move?
qa.a: Telling Kiran everything and answering what was really missing showed the needs (mountains, rest, free weekends), which could be met without quitting or ending the relationship overnight 🙂

qa.q: What might it have been like for Kiran to hear the speech on Sunday morning?
qa.a: Kiran may have felt hurt and shaken, yet chose to listen and ask a question, which turned a possible breakup into an honest talk.

grounding: Illustrates restless drastic thoughts of quitting, leaving and ending a relationship, seen later as a signal of unmet needs that the impulsive plan would not have met.

passage:
'I'm leaving the job. And Pune. Done,' Bhupen said, sinking onto the sofa.
Maa put down the ladle. 'Leaving? What will people say? Who will marry a boy with no job?'
'Maa, please,' said Alka, and sat beside her brother. 'Since when, Bhupen?'
'Since always. Since this morning. I don't know.' He rubbed his eyes. 'I sit in that office and feel like a chair.'
'What's missing?'
He was quiet. 'I used to draw. I used to see people.'
'Okay. So before you quit, can we test something small? A sketch class on Saturday. Ask your manager about one work-from-home day.'
'That's so small, didi.'
'Small is how you find out. If it doesn't help, we'll talk about the big stuff. Properly.'
Maa sniffed, but she brought him tea. Bhupen took out his phone and searched for sketch classes near Kothrud.

qa.q: What does Bhupen say he used to do?
qa.a: He used to draw and to see people.

qa.q: What was Maa worried about when Bhupen said he was leaving?
qa.a: She was afraid of what people would say and whether anyone would marry a boy with no job; her panic came from fear for his future.

qa.q: Why does Alka's approach work better than Maa's first reaction?
qa.a: Alka asks what is missing and suggests small tests, a sketch class and one work-from-home day, which treats his feeling as information rather than a crisis.

qa.q: How might Bhupen experience Alka's questions compared with Maa's reaction?
qa.a: Bhupen likely feels pressured by Maa but heard by Alka; her calm questions let him name what he misses instead of defending himself.

grounding: Shows family members hearing a restless declaration: one panics, while the older sister asks what is missing and suggests small experiments.

passage: Sudha here. I'm writing this down so I remember it. Last month my friend Tanvir called at midnight saying he was selling his bike, quitting the lab and moving to his uncle's farm in Assam. My first answer was, 'You say this every March,' and I nearly hung up to sleep. I'm not proud of that. The next day it bothered me, so I asked him to meet at the tea stall near our old college. I asked what he actually missed. It took him a while. Being outdoors, he said. Using his hands. Not sitting alone at a bench for ten hours. So we made a list of small tries instead: a weekend at the farm first, the community garden on Sundays, asking his supervisor about field sampling. He's tried two of them. He hasn't sold the bike. Listening did more than my joke ever could.

qa.q: Where did Sudha and Tanvir meet the next day?
qa.a: At the tea stall near their old college.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel after brushing off the midnight call?
qa.a: Sudha felt uneasy and a bit ashamed of the dismissive joke, and wanted to make up for it by really listening.

qa.q: What did Sudha change, and why did it help Tanvir?
qa.a: Sudha stopped dismissing him, asked what he missed and helped him list small tries such as a farm weekend and the community garden, so he could test the feeling before making a drastic move.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have felt when Sudha said, 'You say this every March'?
qa.a: Tanvir may have felt brushed aside and more alone, since what he was sharing felt urgent to him.

grounding: Illustrates a friend who first dismisses a restless declaration, then asks what is missing and helps test small changes.

passage: On the train back from her parents' house in Sendai, Aiko opened a notebook and drew a line down the page. Left side: can't change. She wrote: didn't study abroad at twenty; three years at the insurance office. Right side: can still do. Call Professor Mori about the evening translation course. Apologise to Yuki for missing the graduation. She stared at the right column for a while. Then, under both, she wrote a new question: What do I care about when nobody is watching? The answers came slowly. Languages. Being useful to people who are lost. Quiet mornings. Not a big salary, not a title. She texted Yuki: 'Dinner this week? I owe you an apology and a proper talk.'
